cells.tense: The stretch is heavy and you're still in it on purpose, not waiting to be told it's fine.
cells.ask: Pick the one thing you'll carry again tomorrow and say out loud who it's for — strength spent on something named keeps working after the day that took it, and what you carry stays yours when its reason has a name.
cells.core:
You're carrying what's heavy, and you've chosen to keep carrying it. Not because anyone is watching — most of it happens where no one can see — but because it's yours to see through, and you've stopped needing the road to call itself a good road before you walk it. This, not that, and you mean it.

There's a plain shape to the day — up, the load, the flat tyre changed anyway — and it hasn't gone grim on you. What feeds it next is hope, of all things: strength from keeping on wanting something past the point where it's been proven. A flat tyre can't argue with that.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying it on purpose, and the purpose is yours.
cells.verb: persisting through a heavy stretch on strength drawn from inside you, with no one watching
cells.place: the part of a life where you pick a direction and steer toward it on your own say-so, not the part where others come along

cells.tense: The next stretch is already being carried in your head — bracing against weight that hasn't landed, may not land.
cells.ask: Take one trade this week in plain words, out loud — you hold this, that's yours, done — and let both sides of the scale read the weight, so the load you keep comes back at a size a person can hold.
cells.core:
You're out past the end of the week — bracing for the failure that may not come, carrying the bill before it arrives, running the hard conversation through to its worst ending. Steering gets spent ahead of where steering can happen, and the strength that could walk today's road goes into rehearsing a road with no ground under it.

When the wardrobe door still shuts and the shop opens again, endurance is the quiet kind — hold, don't force, it can wait an hour. That kind doesn't ask you to take on a winter's worth today. It carries the load a person can carry at once. Set one of the imagined loads down, and there's a hand free for the real one — fair exchange, without the extra accounting.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding weight nobody has handed you.

cells.tense: A stretch got carried and the strength is behind you now — you're standing where it ended, still facing the weight it held.
cells.ask: Tell one honest listener what it took, in one sentence — the years this held up, the person it held up. What saying it can give back is the first free breath: the load set down where someone can see it had weight. Give it an hour, so it can finish as a real thing that finished.
cells.core:
The strength is spent and behind you — you carried it, and now the hand is open and still shaped like what it held. Direction has gone quiet, so the days run on momentum, and picking a lane feels like it belongs to somebody with more in the tank.

There was a bench in this once — the load set down, not thrown down — and what it produced was a finish, not a collapse: the thing carried got over, and you could let go of it in front of someone, which isn't a defeat. Say what it took, once, where a witness is standing.

cells.tense: You steer the week's hours this way and not that way, and you say it as the plain number of hours rather than the word for a call you've made.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're keeping alive this week, in one sentence to one person — 'this one's mine, I'm holding it.' What saying it can give back is a long stretch made easier by having been said out loud, and the wish heard.
cells.core:
The hours are already being steered — the two you protect, the thing you keep returning to without a name for it — and you call it 'the hours' rather than 'what I'm holding on to.' What you keep is real and unnamed, which is why it doesn't get credit for being the choice it is.

On a good day it's the first inch of green in a hard season — not the harvest, just the stir that says something's coming up, and you can see it as yours. What feeds it is hope: strength from wanting after wanting has gotten expensive. Name the seed as a seed, and it stops pretending to be the season.
cells.sheetLine: You're already steering this. You've just been calling it the hours.
